vignette:
At fifty-one, he still sits with perfect posture at his desk-straight-backed, both feet flat on the floor, hands arranged precisely around the keyboard. It is a posture he learned long ago, in a different kind of room. As a tax inspector for the state, his days are filled with neat columns of numbers, each one fixed and predictable. He likes this. It is one of the few places where he can still feel in control.

The first time she hit him, it was after a dinner party. He was thirty-seven, newly married to a woman whose charm had lit up every room they entered. That night, she accused him of flirting with a coworker. He hadn't. When he tried to deny it, her palm cracked across his cheek. He stood there, stunned, while she cried and begged his forgiveness. He forgave her. For three years, he forgave her.

The abuse came in cycles-brutal, then tender. She would shove him into walls, claw at his arms, throw dishes at his head. One winter, she locked him out of their apartment in his shirtsleeves. He stood in the hallway for four hours, too ashamed to call anyone. His mother had raised him to be strong, to protect his family. Admitting that his wife was hurting him felt like admitting he was not a man. So he told no one. At work, he kept his sleeves long, his explanations vague. He became fastidious with his files, obsessively double-checking every return, because it was the only part of his life he could control.

Now, fourteen years later, he is married to a gentle woman named Linh. He met her after the divorce, and she has never raised her voice at him. He knows he is lucky. But his body does not seem to know.

At home, he cannot bear to have Linh enter a room without warning. If she walks up behind him while he is cooking, he flinches-hard, sometimes enough to drop a spatula. He has learned to keep his back to the kitchen wall, to scan every restaurant before he sits down. The sound of a cabinet slamming shut makes his heart pound so fast he has to grip the counter. Linh has learned to close doors softly, to call his name from across the room before approaching. He hates that she has to do this. He hates himself for needing it.

His nightmares are vivid. In them, she is young again, her face twisted. He wakes up gasping, convinced someone is in the bedroom. Some nights he gets up and runs his hands over the apartment's locks, checking each one twice. He does not tell Linh. Instead, he goes to work early, logs into the taxation system, and buries himself in the quiet logic of audits. He is good at catching discrepancies-a subtle shift in a depreciation schedule, an odd deduction. His colleagues respect his thoroughness. They do not know that his attention to detail is a way of not thinking about his wife's hands around his throat.

He avoids arguments at all costs. When clients become angry on the phone, he feels a cold dread rise in his chest. He talks softer, lowers his head, agrees to extensions he should not grant. Afterward, he feels sick. He knows he is not in danger anymore, but his mind does not care.

Last week, Linh asked why he still sleeps on the far edge of the bed, as if ready to flee. He said he was just a light sleeper. She did not push. She is patient. But he watches her sometimes, when she is reading, and he feels a deep, hollow sadness. He wants to tell her everything-how small he felt, how he used to beg her to stop, how he still hears her voice in certain silences. But the words stay locked. He returns to his tax returns, to the clean rows of numbers, the only truth he can still arrange.
